newsitem.title: UK: Euro products outlook - Gas oil still dominant.
newsitem.headline: Euro products outlook - Gas oil still dominant.

text.p: Gas oil will continue to dominate European oil products markets this week, with jitters over the expiry of the IPE September futures contract on Thursday and tight supply expected to push prices higher, traders said. "I can't take my eyes off gas oil," a gasoline trader said.
The September IPE contract settled at $7 higher $220.00 a tonne on Friday.

Tight prompt availability in the heating oil barge market, fears of a squeeze on the September IPE contract ahead of its expiry on Thursday and growing end-user demand in Germany will keep gas oil in the limelight, traders said.
"People are clamouring for heating oil," a U.K.-based refinery trader said. "German end-users are finally coming round to the fact that prices are not going to come off."
German household stocks are currently at historically low levels at below 50 percent of tank capacity.
Gasoline traders said the fact refiners were maximising on distillate production to cash in on the high gas oil prices would prop up an otherwise lacklustre gasoline market.
Gasoline barge prices are expected to remain steady to firm.
Both eurograde and regular supplies have tightened in Rotterdam due to refinery maintenance and the maximisation of distillate production.
Traders said the tightness would be balanced out by slack buying in Europe. Tight U.S. supplies were expected to hold prices there reasonably firm and the arbitrage door ajar.

Narrow transatlantic arbitrage options saw U.S. regular and superplus grades fob U.K. barely holding steady with a U.K. refiner offering M4 at Oct NYMEX -6 cents a gallon on Friday compared with trade at -6.75 cents earlier in the week.
Traders said naphtha direction remains dependant on crude, with the spot market looking fairly balanced.

Some enquiry may be seen from petrochemical end-users seeking an alternative to high priced LPG feedstock and refiners could resume efforts to find platformer feedstocks although little fresh supply of N+A material is seen.
On the fuel oil market, traders said the unusually narrow differential seen recently between high and low sulphur fuel oil should start to widen over the next few weeks.
Firm high sulphur prices, boosted by robust demand and limited supply, look set to come under pressure as more cargoes emerge later in the month.
Traders said there was a possibility Mediterranean cargoes could move into northern Europe, while at least five Russian cargoes out of the Baltic were seen on offer.

Low sulphur markets look better supplied and traders say current prices have been pressured lower by a number of key players. Much depends, however, on the purchasing needs of Italian state utility ENEL.
